name: Hydrogen gas
blurb: Each hydrogen has 1 hand. They hold hands, and now neither has an empty hand. The lightest molecule there is.
uses: Adding hydrogen to fuels at refineries, ammonia, fuel cells, liquid hydrogen rocket fuel.

lens.rocket: Liquid H2 (-253 °C) gets the most push per pound of any common rocket propellant. But it's so light that it needs huge tanks.
lens.nexus: Hydrogen is the scarce ingredient at your plant. Polyethylene has only 2 H per carbon, so not every broken piece can fill its hands and become methane.

facts: About 9 of every 10 atoms in the universe are hydrogen. Nearly all of it was made in the first minutes after the Big Bang.
The Sun shines by squeezing hydrogen into helium, about 600 million tons every second.
The Hindenburg airship was filled with hydrogen because the US would not sell Germany helium.
rankWhy: Used to make ammonia and to clean up fuels at refineries. A possible clean fuel.

name: Oxygen gas
blurb: Each oxygen has 2 hands. They hold both hands with each other: a double bond.
uses: Breathing, burning, steelmaking, and liquid oxygen (LOX), what rocket fuel burns with.

lens.rocket: Liquid oxygen is most of the weight of a methane or kerosene rocket. Raptor reportedly burns about 3.6 kg of oxygen per kg of methane.

facts: Liquid oxygen is pale blue, and it gets pulled toward a strong magnet.
By weight, oxygen is the most common element in Earth's crust, a bit under half of all rock.
Almost all the oxygen in the air was made by plants, algae and tiny ocean microbes using sunlight.
rankWhy: About a fifth of the air. You breathe it, and every fire burns with it.

name: Ozone
blurb: Three oxygens can't all hold hands in a simple, even way. So the shared electrons smear across all three. That awkward grip makes it quick to react.
uses: High-up shield against the sun's UV; cleaning and disinfecting water.
facts: If all the ozone high in the sky were squeezed to ground-level pressure, it would make a layer only about 3 mm thick. That's about two pennies stacked.
Its name comes from a Greek word meaning 'to smell.' The sharp, clean smell near a lightning storm can be ozone.
rankWhy: High up, the ozone layer shields life from harmful sunlight.

name: Nitrogen gas
blurb: Each nitrogen has 3 hands, and they hold all three at once: a triple bond. It's one of the strongest bonds in chemistry. That's why N2 barely reacts.
uses: 78% of air; a do-nothing gas used to blanket reactors and tanks.

lens.nexus: At Nexus, nitrogen is flushed through the reactors to push oxygen out. So plastic breaks apart instead of burning.
lens.rocket: Nitrogen gas flushes out lines. It's also the gas pushed out of simple cold-gas thrusters.

facts: Liquid nitrogen boils at -196 °C. One cup of it turns into roughly 700 cups of gas.
Every breath you take is mostly nitrogen, and your body breathes it right back out unused.
Plants can't use it straight from the air either. Lightning and special soil bacteria are nature's main ways to crack that triple bond.
rankWhy: Most of the air. It's also the raw ingredient for all nitrogen fertilizer.

name: Chlorine gas
blurb: Each chlorine has 1 hand. Two chlorines hold hands, and both are satisfied.
uses: Making PVC, cleaning drinking water, bleach.
facts: Chlorine is a yellow-green gas. Its name comes from the Greek word for pale green.
In 1915 at Ypres, chlorine became the first poison gas used on a large scale in war.
Adding chlorine to drinking water in the early 1900s is a big reason diseases like cholera and typhoid became rare.
rankWhy: Keeps drinking water safe and is needed to make PVC.

name: Fluorine gas
blurb: Like chlorine, each has 1 hand, so they hold hands once. Fluorine tugs on electrons harder than any element. So F2 attacks almost anything.
uses: Making uranium hexafluoride, sulfur hexafluoride (SF6) and other fluorine chemicals.
facts: Fluorine was so hard to isolate that several chemists were hurt trying. Henri Moissan finally did it in 1886 and later won a Nobel Prize.
It reacts with nearly every element, even the noble gas xenon.
The fluoride in toothpaste is fluorine that has already grabbed an extra electron, so it's calm instead of wild.

name: Bromine
blurb: Each bromine has 1 hand, so two of them hold hands. It's a liquid at room temperature.
uses: Fire-slowing additives, drilling fluids, water treatment.
facts: Bromine and mercury are the only two elements that are liquid at room temperature.
Its name comes from the Greek word for stench. It has a harsh, choking smell.
Royal purple, the ancient dye made from sea snails, has bromine in it.

name: Iodine
blurb: Each iodine has 1 hand, so two hold hands. The atoms are big and soft, so it's a solid that turns straight into purple vapor.
uses: Germ killer, iodized salt, helping insides show up on X-rays.
facts: Iodine was discovered in 1811 by a French chemist who was making gunpowder ingredients from seaweed ash.
Your thyroid gland needs iodine. Adding it to salt, starting in the US in 1924, made goiter (a swollen neck) rare.
Its name comes from the Greek word for violet, the color of its vapor.

name: Methane
blurb: Carbon has 4 hands and no other carbon to hold. So all 4 hands grab hydrogens. Every hand held: the most settled shape for one carbon.
uses: Natural gas fuel, making hydrogen, rocket fuel.

lens.nexus: The smallest thing your plant makes. It stays a gas even when cooled, and is usually burned to heat the reactor.
lens.rocket: Raptor's fuel. It burns clean (little soot or carbon gunk) and can be made on Mars with the Sabatier reaction.

facts: Natural gas has no smell. Gas companies add a sulfur chemical that smells like rotten eggs so you notice a leak.
Cows burp out methane made by microbes living in their stomachs.
Saturn's moon Titan is so cold that it has lakes and rain made of liquid methane.
rankWhy: Natural gas: heats homes, makes electricity, and starts the chain to fertilizer and plastics.

name: Ethane
blurb: Two carbons hold hands using one hand each. Each carbon has 3 hands left, and each grabs a hydrogen.
uses: Main raw material for US ethane 'crackers', plants that turn it into ethylene.

lens.nexus: Cheap shale ethane is why most US crackers run on ethane, not naphtha (a light oil). Your plant's oil can stand in for naphtha, so it fits crackers fed on liquid.

facts: Ethane boils at about -89 °C, so on Earth it's always a gas. On frozen Titan it pools in lakes with methane.
It comes out of the ground mixed into natural gas, then gets separated and piped to crackers.

name: Ethylene
blurb: Each carbon holds 2 hydrogens and the other carbon, with one hand left. So they hold hands twice: a C=C double bond. That second grip is the 'handle' for linking into plastic chains.
uses: The building block of polyethylene; the most-made carbon-based chemical.

lens.nexus: Cracking pulls hydrogen off ethane to make ethylene. Then ethylenes get linked into polyethylene. Your plant partly runs that backwards. But polyethylene breaks into many sizes, not mostly back to ethylene.

facts: Plants make ethylene as a ripening signal. One ripe banana in a bag speeds up the other fruit around it.
Fruit companies pump ethylene into warehouse 'ripening rooms' to time when bananas turn yellow.
rankWhy: The most-made building block in the plastics industry.

name: Acetylene
blurb: Each carbon holds just 1 hydrogen, leaving 3 hands free. So the carbons hold all 3: a triple bond. Lots of stored energy.
uses: Welding and cutting torches with oxygen (about 3,100 °C flame).
facts: Pure acetylene is unsafe to squeeze into a tank. Welding cylinders are packed with a spongy filler soaked in acetone, and the acetylene dissolves into it.
Old miners' lamps made acetylene by dripping water onto rocks of calcium carbide, then burned the gas for light.

name: Propane
blurb: Three carbons in a row. End carbons hold 3 H, the middle one 2.
uses: Heating and grill fuel (LPG), raw material for propylene.

lens.nexus: Part of the light gas that comes off your plant's reactor.

facts: Propane is heavier than air. A leak sinks and collects in low spots like basements.
It boils at about -42 °C. Grill tanks hold it as a liquid under pressure, and it boils into gas when you open the valve.
rankWhy: Grill and heating gas, and a fuel for forklifts.

name: Propylene
blurb: Three carbons; two hold hands twice. That double grip is where polypropylene chains link.

lens.nexus: Like ethylene, it stays a gas at room temperature. It leaves with the gases that don't turn to liquid.

facts: After ethylene, propylene is the second most important building block for plastics.
Refinery units that crack heavy oil into gasoline make lots of propylene on the side.
rankWhy: The second big plastics building block after ethylene.

name: Butane
blurb: 4 carbons in a row, spare hands all on H. Straight chains (alkanes) follow CnH(2n+2).
facts: You can see butane sloshing as a liquid in a clear lighter. A little pressure keeps it liquid at room temperature.
It boils at about -1 °C, so a lighter left in freezing cold may barely light.
Its branched twin, isobutane, has the same atoms. It's the cooling gas in many home fridges.

name: 1,3-Butadiene
blurb: 4 carbons; two pairs hold hands twice (two double bonds).
facts: In World War II, Japan cut off most natural rubber. The US built a huge industry making synthetic rubber from butadiene.
It's also the 'B' in ABS, the tough plastic LEGO bricks are made from.

name: Octane (iso-octane)
blurb: 8 carbons in a branched shape. Branching resists engine knock, which is where the 'octane rating' comes from.

lens.nexus: Gasoline-size molecules (C5-C12) are part of what your plant's oil can be refined into.

facts: The octane scale runs from heptane (0) to iso-octane (100). A fuel rated 90 knocks like a mix of 90% iso-octane and 10% heptane.
Some fuels score above 100, like racing fuels and pure ethanol.
rankWhy: The standard for gasoline. An octane rating compares fuel to it.

name: Dodecane (RP-1 stand-in)
blurb: 12 carbons holding hands in a line. Kerosene and RP-1 are mixes of molecules around this size.
uses: Jet fuel and rocket kerosene size.

lens.rocket: RP-1 is very pure kerosene, burned by Falcon 9's Merlin engines. Long chains can leave carbon gunk (coking) in engines. That's one reason Starship chose methane.
lens.nexus: Diesel- and kerosene-size chains (about C10-C20) cool into liquid oil at your plant.

facts: Twelve-carbon chains boil around 216 °C, far hotter than gasoline-size molecules.
Jet fuel and RP-1 are cousins. RP-1 is held to tighter limits on sulfur and ring-shaped molecules, which helps keep rocket engines clean.

name: Hexadecane (cetane)
blurb: 16 carbons holding hands in a line. It's the yardstick for how well diesel ignites (the cetane number).

lens.nexus: Middle of your oil range. Much longer chains (C20+) are wax.

facts: Diesel engines have no spark plugs. They squeeze air until it's hot enough to light the fuel by itself.
Rudolf Diesel showed an engine running on peanut oil at the 1900 Paris World's Fair.
Hexadecane turns solid at about 18 °C. Long waxy chains like it are why diesel can gel in winter.

name: Benzene
blurb: Six carbons hold hands in a ring, each also holding one hydrogen. Each has one spare hand, shared around the whole ring. That makes it very stable.
uses: Starting point for styrene, nylon, plastics, dyes.

lens.nexus: In the reactor's heat, broken pieces can curl up into rings like this (aromatics). They are a step on the road to char.

facts: Michael Faraday discovered benzene in 1825, in oily leftovers from the gas used for lamps.
August Kekulé said the ring shape came to him in a daydream of a snake biting its own tail.
Benzene can cause cancer, so it's kept to tiny amounts in gasoline.
rankWhy: Starting ring for nylon, polystyrene, dyes and many medicines.

name: Toluene
blurb: A benzene ring holding a methyl (CH3) group.
facts: TNT is toluene with three nitro groups added. Its full name is trinitrotoluene.
It was first found in tolu balsam, a South American tree sap, which gave it its name.

name: Styrene
blurb: Benzene ring plus a C=C (vinyl) handle for linking up.
uses: Building block of polystyrene and ABS.

lens.nexus: Heated, polystyrene mostly unzips back to styrene, like a zipper. Polyethylene instead snaps at random spots.

facts: Tiny natural amounts of styrene show up in foods like cinnamon, strawberries and coffee.
It also goes into SBR, a synthetic rubber used in many car tires.

name: Naphthalene
blurb: Two benzene rings joined at an edge. As more rings join, hydrogen per carbon drops toward zero.
uses: Mothballs, a starting point for dyes.

lens.nexus: Joined rings are how char grows. Keep stripping hydrogen and joining rings, and you head toward graphite-like carbon.

facts: Mothballs slowly turn from solid straight into gas. Those fumes are what keep moths away.
It was one of the first chemicals pulled out of coal tar, back in the early 1800s.

name: Polyethylene
blurb: Ethylene lets go of its second grip. Each carbon uses that freed hand to grab the next one, over and over. Shown: a 6-carbon slice of a chain thousands of carbons long.
uses: Bags, films, bottles, pipe. The most common plastic.

lens.nexus: Your plant's main feed. Heat breaks the carbon-carbon grips (weaker than carbon-hydrogen) at random spots. That gives gas, oil, wax and char.

facts: It was discovered by accident in 1933 at the British company ICI, when a high-pressure test left a waxy white solid.
In World War II it insulated radar cables. That made radar light enough to fit in airplanes.
rankWhy: The most common plastic: bags, bottles, films and pipes.

name: Polypropylene
blurb: Polyethylene's chain, with a CH3 branch on every other carbon.

lens.nexus: Breaks apart a bit more easily than polyethylene, because the branch points are weak spots.

facts: It can bend thousands of times without snapping, so it's used for 'living hinges' like flip-top bottle caps.
Australia made the first plastic banknotes in 1988, printed on polypropylene film.
Giulio Natta, who figured out how to make it in a neat, orderly form, shared the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
rankWhy: Second most common plastic: food tubs, car parts, bottle caps.

name: Polystyrene
blurb: A chain of carbons holding hands, with a benzene ring hanging off every other carbon.
facts: Foam polystyrene is about 98% air. That trapped air is why a foam cup keeps coffee hot.
The real 'Styrofoam' brand is blue building insulation. White foam cups are a different product people call by the same name.

name: PVC
blurb: Polyethylene, but every other carbon holds a chlorine in one hand instead of a hydrogen.

lens.nexus: A problem for your plant. Heating it releases HCl, which eats away equipment. It must be kept out of the feed.

facts: By weight, PVC is more than half chlorine.
PVC was stiff and brittle at first. In 1926 Waldo Semon at B.F. Goodrich found how to make it soft and bendy.
That soft PVC shows up in garden hoses, shower curtains and fake leather.
rankWhy: Pipes, window frames, flooring and cable coating.

name: PTFE (Teflon)
blurb: Every hydrogen is swapped for fluorine. Carbon and fluorine grip harder than almost any one-hand hold. So almost nothing sticks or reacts.
uses: Non-stick coatings, seals, liners that resist chemicals.

lens.rocket: Used for seals and liners that must survive liquid oxygen.

facts: Roy Plunkett found it by accident in 1938. A gas tank seemed empty, and inside was a slippery white powder.
It helped build the first atomic bombs, because it could survive the harsh uranium gas used to enrich uranium.
Even geckos can't stick to it.

name: PET
blurb: Rings and ester links (C-O-C=O) in the chain. Those oxygens make it act very differently from polyethylene.

lens.nexus: Usually unwanted at your plant. Its oxygen ends up as CO2, water and acids instead of oil.

facts: Nathaniel Wyeth patented the PET soda bottle in 1973. His brother was the famous painter Andrew Wyeth.
The same plastic in a water bottle can be spun into fleece jackets and carpet.
rankWhy: Water and soda bottles, and polyester clothing.

name: Water
blurb: Oxygen has 2 hands, and each holds a hydrogen. Oxygen also keeps two pairs of electrons to itself. They push the H's into a bent shape.

lens.rocket: The main thing coming out of hydrogen and methane engines.
lens.nexus: Wet feed at your plant steals heat and adds oxygen to the products.

facts: Water expands about 9% when it freezes, so ice floats. Most solids sink in their own liquid.
Water is heaviest at about 4 °C, so lakes freeze from the top down and fish survive underneath.
The space station recycles about 98% of its water, including astronaut sweat and urine.
rankWhy: Every living thing runs on it, and it covers most of the planet.

name: Hydrogen peroxide
blurb: Two oxygens hold hands, and that O-O grip is weak. It snaps easily, giving off oxygen and heat.
uses: Bleaching, killing germs, single-ingredient rocket fuel (high-test peroxide).

lens.rocket: High-test peroxide breaks down over silver, a catalyst (a helper that isn't used up), into hot steam and oxygen. Used in early rockets and thrusters.

facts: The bombardier beetle mixes hydrogen peroxide with other chemicals to shoot a boiling-hot spray at attackers.
The 1960s Bell Rocket Belt jetpack ran on hydrogen peroxide. It could only fly for about 20 seconds.
Drugstore peroxide is about 3%. Rocket-grade peroxide is often around 90%.
rankWhy: Bleaches paper and cleans cuts. Breaks down into just water and oxygen.

name: Carbon monoxide
blurb: Carbon and oxygen hold hands three times: a very strong triple bond. It forms when there isn't enough oxygen to make CO2.
uses: Syngas (a gas mix for making chemicals and methanol); poisonous.
facts: It has no color, smell or taste. That's why homes need CO alarms.
Your blood grabs carbon monoxide about 200 times more tightly than oxygen. So even a little crowds out the oxygen.
In a blast furnace, CO is what pulls the oxygen off iron ore to leave iron.
rankWhy: Poison gas from bad burning. Industry uses it to make steel and chemicals.

name: Carbon dioxide
blurb: Each oxygen has 2 hands and holds both with carbon. Two double grips use all 4 of carbon's hands.
uses: Fizzy drinks, dry ice, plant food; main greenhouse gas.

lens.rocket: Mars' air is about 95% CO2. That's the carbon source for making methane there.

facts: Dry ice is frozen CO2 at -78.5 °C. It turns straight into gas without melting first.
Mars has polar caps topped with frozen CO2 that grow and shrink with the seasons.
Warm soda goes flat faster because warm water holds less dissolved gas.
rankWhy: What breathing and burning give off, what plants eat, and the main gas behind climate change.

name: Methanol
blurb: Methane, but one of carbon's hands holds an OH group instead of a hydrogen.
facts: It's called wood alcohol because it was first made by heating wood without air. That's pyrolysis, the same basic idea your plant uses on plastic.
It burns with a nearly invisible flame in daylight. Indy cars ran on it for years, which made pit fires hard to see.
Drinking even a small amount can cause blindness.
rankWhy: A basic building block for plastics, glues and fuels.

name: Ethanol
blurb: Ethane, but one end holds an OH instead of a hydrogen.
facts: Yeast makes ethanol by eating sugar. Beer, wine and corn fuel ethanol all come from that same process.
Most US gasoline has about 10% ethanol mixed in, labeled E10.
Henry Ford's Model T could run on ethanol as well as gasoline.
rankWhy: In every alcoholic drink and blended into gasoline as fuel.

name: Dimethyl ether
blurb: Same atoms as ethanol, but oxygen sits in the middle: an isomer.
facts: DME boils at about -24 °C, while ethanol, with the very same atoms, boils at 78 °C.
Moving the oxygen to the middle removes the OH 'sticky end' that makes ethanol molecules cling to each other.

name: Formaldehyde
blurb: Carbon holds oxygen with 2 hands and a hydrogen in each other hand.
facts: Your own body makes small amounts of formaldehyde as part of normal chemistry.
That new-furniture smell can include formaldehyde slowly leaking from glues in pressed wood.

name: Acetic acid
blurb: A methyl (CH3) group holding hands with a carboxylic acid (COOH) group.
uses: Vinegar, making PET and vinyl acetate.
facts: Vinegar is mostly water with about 4 to 8% acetic acid.
Pure acetic acid freezes at about 17 °C, a cool room. The icy-looking crystals are why it's called 'glacial' acetic acid.
rankWhy: Vinegar, and a building block for PET plastic and paints.

name: Acetone
blurb: A C=O carbon holding a methyl group on each side.
facts: Your body makes acetone when it burns fat for fuel, like during fasting. It can show up on your breath.
In World War I, Chaim Weizmann found a way to make acetone with bacteria, which Britain needed for explosives. He later became Israel's first president.

name: Ethylene glycol
blurb: Ethane, but each end holds an OH instead of a hydrogen.
facts: It tastes sweet but is poisonous. Many antifreeze brands now add a bitter chemical so pets and kids won't drink it.
A 50/50 mix with water won't freeze until about -37 °C.

name: Glucose
blurb: A ring of 5 carbons and 1 oxygen, with OH groups all around.
uses: Blood sugar; building block of starch and cellulose.
facts: Your brain is about 2% of your body weight but uses about 20% of your energy, mostly from glucose.
Starch and cellulose are both chains of glucose. A small change in how the links point is why you can digest bread but not wood.
rankWhy: The sugar every cell burns for energy. Plants make it from sunlight.

name: Ammonia
blurb: Nitrogen has 3 hands, each holding a hydrogen. It keeps one pair of electrons to itself, on top.
facts: Fritz Haber and Carl Bosch learned to make ammonia from air in the early 1900s. Fertilizer from their process helps feed about half the people on Earth.
Roughly half the nitrogen atoms in your body passed through an ammonia factory first.
The X-15 rocket plane burned ammonia with liquid oxygen.
rankWhy: Made from air and natural gas. Fertilizer from it helps feed a large share of humanity.

name: Hydrogen cyanide
blurb: Carbon holds nitrogen with 3 hands (a triple bond) and a hydrogen with its 4th.
uses: Starting point for nylon and acrylic; very poisonous.
facts: Cyanide smells like bitter almonds to some people. Many others can't smell it at all because of their genes.
Apple seeds and peach pits hold a chemical that can release small amounts of HCN when chewed.

name: Nitrous oxide
blurb: A straight N-N-O chain with charge spread across it.
uses: Anesthetic, whipped cream propellant, oxygen source for hybrid rockets.

lens.rocket: The oxygen source in hybrid rocket motors. It builds its own tank pressure.

facts: In 1799 Humphry Davy tested laughing gas on himself and his friends. It later became one of the first anesthetics.
Under pressure it dissolves into cream's fat. When sprayed out, it puffs up and makes the cream fluffy.

name: Nitrogen dioxide
blurb: An odd number of electrons, so one hand is always left empty. That makes it a reactive radical.
uses: Part of smog; making nitric acid.
facts: NO2 is the brown haze in smoggy city air.
Car engines make it by accident. The heat is so high that nitrogen and oxygen from the air join up.
Catalytic converters exist partly to turn it back into harmless nitrogen.

name: Dinitrogen tetroxide
blurb: Two NO2 molecules each have one empty hand. They grab each other, making an N-N bond.
uses: Rocket oxygen source that stores well.

lens.rocket: With hydrazine fuels it catches fire on contact (hypergolic), so no igniter is needed. Used on Dragon's Draco thrusters.

facts: N2O4 and NO2 keep switching back and forth. Cold favors colorless N2O4, and warmth turns it into brown NO2.
The Apollo service module engine burned it with a hydrazine fuel blend. Since it lit on contact, there was no igniter to fail.

name: Hydrazine
blurb: Two nitrogens hold hands. Each uses its other 2 hands to hold hydrogens.
uses: Single-ingredient satellite thruster fuel, foaming agents.

lens.rocket: Breaks down into hot gas over iridium, a catalyst (a helper that isn't used up). The classic satellite thruster fuel.

facts: The Voyager probes use hydrazine thrusters to keep their antennas pointed at Earth. In 2017, engineers fired Voyager 1 backup thrusters that had sat unused for 37 years.
It's so toxic that crews fueling spacecraft wear full protective suits.

name: Monomethylhydrazine
blurb: Hydrazine, but one hand holds a methyl (CH3) group instead of a hydrogen.
uses: Storable rocket fuel that lights on contact.

lens.rocket: Paired with N2O4 in spacecraft thrusters such as Dragon's Draco and SuperDraco.

facts: The Space Shuttle's orbital maneuvering engines burned MMH with N2O4.
Plain hydrazine freezes at about 2 °C. Adding the methyl group drops that to about -52 °C, handy in cold space.

name: Urea
blurb: A C=O carbon with two NH2 groups.
facts: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea from non-living chemicals. That broke the old belief that only living things could make such compounds.
Your body makes urea to get rid of extra nitrogen. Its name comes from urine, where it leaves.
Diesel exhaust fluid is 32.5% urea in water. Sprayed into hot exhaust, it helps turn smog gases into plain nitrogen and water.
rankWhy: The world's most-used nitrogen fertilizer. Your body makes it too.

name: Nitric acid
blurb: Nitrogen holds three oxygens. One of them also holds the hydrogen.
facts: Mixed with hydrochloric acid, it makes aqua regia, one of the few liquids that dissolves gold.
In 1940 a chemist hid two gold Nobel medals from the Nazis by dissolving them in aqua regia. After the war the gold was recovered and the medals were recast.
Most of it is made by burning ammonia over a platinum mesh.
rankWhy: Turns ammonia into fertilizer and explosives.

name: Hydrogen sulfide
blurb: Sulfur, like oxygen, has 2 hands. Each holds a hydrogen.
uses: Rotten-egg gas in sour crude and natural gas; where refinery sulfur comes from.

lens.nexus: Sulfur in your plant's feed ends up as H2S and other sulfur chemicals. They must be scrubbed out of the gas and oil.

facts: You can smell tiny traces of it, but high levels knock out your sense of smell. So a smell that fades can mean danger.
Rotten eggs smell this way because bacteria break down the sulfur in egg proteins.

name: Sulfur dioxide
blurb: Sulfur is bigger, so it can hold out extra hands. It holds each oxygen with 2 hands.
uses: Making sulfuric acid, keeping food fresh; a cause of acid rain.
facts: After Mount Pinatubo erupted in 1991, its sulfur dioxide cooled the whole planet by about 0.5 °C for a while.
The sharp smell of a just-struck match is partly sulfur dioxide.

name: Sulfuric acid
blurb: Sulfur in the middle holds four oxygens. Two of them also hold a hydrogen.
uses: The most-made industrial chemical: fertilizer, batteries, refining.
facts: A country's sulfuric acid output was once used as a measure of how industrial it was.
It pulls water out of sugar so hard that the sugar turns into a tall, steaming column of black carbon.
The clouds of Venus are made of sulfuric acid droplets.
rankWhy: Made in larger amounts than almost any other chemical. Used for fertilizer, metals and batteries.

name: Hydrogen chloride
blurb: 1 hand each, so they hold hands once. In water it becomes hydrochloric acid.

lens.nexus: Given off when PVC is heated. That's why PVC is screened out of your plant's feed.

facts: Your stomach makes hydrochloric acid. Stomach juice has a pH around 1.5 to 3.5.
A thick layer of mucus keeps that acid from eating your stomach wall.
rankWhy: Your stomach acid. Industry uses it to clean steel and make PVC.

name: Hydrogen fluoride
blurb: They hold hands once, but fluorine tugs the handshake hard toward itself.
uses: Etching glass, alkylation in refineries, fluorine chemicals.

lens.nexus: Some refineries use HF as the catalyst (helper) in alkylation, a step that builds high-octane gasoline.

facts: HF is called a 'weak' acid, but it's one of the most dangerous. It slips through skin and pulls calcium out of the body.
Almost all fluorine chemicals, from Teflon to refrigerants, start out as HF.

name: Carbon tetrachloride
blurb: Methane's shape, but carbon's 4 hands hold chlorines instead of hydrogens.
uses: Once a solvent and used to make refrigerants; now restricted.
facts: It was once used in fire extinguishers. But on hot surfaces it can form phosgene, a poison gas, so it was dropped.
It also harms the ozone layer, so it's controlled by the Montreal Protocol treaty.

name: Tetrafluoromethane
blurb: Carbon's 4 hands each hold a fluorine. Extremely stable.
facts: CF4 is one of the longest-lasting gases known. Once released, it stays in the air for about 50,000 years.
Aluminum smelters give off small amounts of CF4 as a by-product.

name: Chloroform
blurb: Carbon's 4 hands hold one hydrogen and three chlorines.
facts: In 1853 Dr. John Snow gave Queen Victoria chloroform while she gave birth. That made pain relief in childbirth popular.
Movies show it knocking someone out in seconds. In real life it takes minutes and can easily kill.

name: Phosphine
blurb: Phosphorus, like nitrogen, has 3 hands. Each holds a hydrogen.
facts: In 2020 scientists reported possible signs of phosphine in Venus's clouds. The finding is still being debated.
Impure phosphine smells like garlic or rotting fish.

name: Phosphorus trichloride
blurb: Phosphorus's 3 hands each hold a chlorine.
facts: It reacts with water so fast that it fumes in damp air, giving off HCl.
Phosphorus has 3 hands like nitrogen, so PCl3 is shaped like a short pyramid, just like ammonia.

name: Sulfur hexafluoride
blurb: Sulfur is big enough to hold out 6 hands, more than the usual rule. Extremely stable.
facts: SF6 is about 5 times heavier than air. Breathing it makes your voice sound very deep, the opposite of helium.
A foil boat can float on an invisible pool of SF6 gas in a fish tank.
It's the strongest greenhouse gas known, about 23,500 times stronger than CO2 pound for pound over 100 years.

name: Silane
blurb: Silicon sits below carbon, so it also has 4 hands, each holding a hydrogen: silicon's methane.
uses: Making ultra-pure silicon for chips and solar cells.
facts: Silane catches fire by itself in air, so a leak at a chip plant can burn with no spark at all.
Silicon can't build long, stable chains the way carbon can. That's one reason life is built on carbon.

name: Triethylborane
blurb: Boron has only 3 hands, so it holds 3 groups. Even then it has a gap that wants electrons. That hunger is why it catches fire on contact with air.
uses: Igniter that catches fire by itself in air.

lens.rocket: The TEB in TEA-TEB, which lights Falcon 9's Merlin engines with a green flash.

facts: The SR-71 Blackbird spy plane also used TEB to light its engines. It carried only enough for a limited number of starts.
Boron is what gives TEB's flame its green color.

name: Triethylaluminium
blurb: Aluminum, like boron, holds with 3 hands but still has a gap that wants electrons. So it reacts violently with oxygen and water.

lens.rocket: The TEA in TEA-TEB igniter on Falcon 9.
lens.nexus: Teams up with titanium catalysts (Ziegler-Natta) to make polyethylene and polypropylene.

facts: Karl Ziegler's work with aluminum compounds like this earned him a share of the 1963 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
Each Merlin engine relight uses up a shot of TEA-TEB, so the supply limits how many times it can restart.

name: Xenon difluoride
blurb: Xenon has 0 hands. But it's big, with outer electrons far from its center, so fluorine can tug them into handshakes anyway.
uses: Adds fluorine to other chemicals; etching silicon.
facts: Before 1962, textbooks said noble gases could never form compounds. Neil Bartlett proved them wrong with xenon.
XeF2 is a stable solid that forms colorless crystals you can keep in a bottle.

name: Xenon tetrafluoride
blurb: Four fluorines around xenon in a flat square.
uses: Proof that noble gases aren't totally inert.
facts: XeF4 was first made in 1962, the same year as Bartlett's discovery, by heating xenon with fluorine.
Xenon keeps two pairs of electrons to itself, one above and one below. They push the four fluorines into that flat square.

name: Nickel carbonyl
blurb: Four CO molecules each give nickel both halves of a handshake. Very poisonous gas.
facts: Ludwig Mond discovered it around 1890. It was the first known compound of a metal bonded to carbon monoxide.
It boils at only 43 °C. So nickel can be carried off as a gas, then dropped back out as pure metal by heating.

name: Ammonium perchlorate
blurb: A solid of charged pieces, NH4+ and ClO4-, stuck together like magnets. The ClO4- carries 4 oxygens ready to hand over.
uses: Oxygen source in solid rocket boosters (mixed with aluminum powder).

lens.rocket: Shuttle SRBs and SLS boosters burn ammonium perchlorate with aluminum powder in a rubbery binder.

facts: In 1988 a Nevada factory making ammonium perchlorate for the Space Shuttle blew up in a series of huge explosions.
NASA's Phoenix lander found perchlorates in Martian soil in 2008.

name: Sodium chloride
blurb: Sodium would rather give away its 1 loose electron. Chlorine has 1 empty hand and takes it. Now Na+ and Cl- stick like magnets in a grid, not as molecules.
uses: Table salt; source of chlorine and sodium hydroxide.
facts: Sodium is a metal that bursts into flame in water, and chlorine is a poison gas. Together they make something you sprinkle on food.
Each grain of table salt is a tiny cube, because its grid of atoms is cube-shaped.
rankWhy: Table salt. Your body needs it, and it's the starting point for chlorine and lye.

name: Potassium chloride
blurb: Same as table salt: one electron handed over.
facts: Bananas are rich in potassium, and a tiny share of all potassium is naturally radioactive.
'Potash' means pot ash. Early settlers made potassium salts by soaking wood ashes in pots.
rankWhy: Potash: the main way farms get potassium. Also a salt substitute.

name: Lithium fluoride
blurb: Lithium gives 1, fluorine takes 1.
facts: In the 1960s, Oak Ridge ran a test nuclear reactor using a melted salt made with lithium fluoride.
Unlike table salt, it barely dissolves in water.

name: Magnesium oxide
blurb: Magnesium gives away 2 electrons; oxygen's 2 empty hands take them. Double charges grip hard, so it melts at about 2,800 °C.
facts: Burning magnesium ribbon makes a blinding white flash. The white ash left behind is MgO.
MgO bricks line steel furnaces that hold molten steel at over 1,500 °C.

name: Calcium oxide
blurb: Calcium gives 2 electrons; oxygen takes 2.
facts: Heated in a hot flame, quicklime glows bright white. Old theaters used it for stage lights, which is where 'in the limelight' comes from.
Adding water to quicklime gives off enough heat to boil the water.
Cement plants make it by baking limestone, which releases CO2. That's a big part of cement's carbon footprint.
rankWhy: Lime: comes from limestone and goes into cement, steelmaking and water treatment.

name: Calcium fluoride
blurb: Calcium gives away 2 electrons, so it takes 2 fluorines (1 each).
facts: Fluorite gave its name to both fluorine and the word 'fluorescence,' because some pieces glow under UV light.
Its name comes from the Latin word 'to flow.' Metal workers added it to help melted metal and slag flow.

name: Magnesium chloride
blurb: Magnesium gives 2 electrons, so it pairs with 2 chlorines.
facts: The Dead Sea is unusually rich in magnesium chloride.
Tofu makers use it, called nigari in Japan, to curdle soy milk.

name: Calcium chloride
blurb: Calcium gives 2, each chlorine takes 1.
facts: Dissolving it in water gives off heat, which helps it melt ice even in deep cold.
It pulls so much water from the air that a pile left out can dissolve into a puddle by itself.

name: Aluminum oxide
blurb: Aluminum gives away 3 electrons; oxygen takes 2. The smallest even match is 2 Al to 3 O (6 electrons each way).
uses: Sapphire, grinding grit, catalyst supports, the protective skin on aluminum.

lens.nexus: Alumina is a common base for catalysts (reaction helpers), and part of zeolite and clay catalysts.
lens.rocket: The white smoke from solid rocket boosters is mostly aluminum oxide particles.

facts: Rubies and sapphires are both aluminum oxide. A trace of chromium makes red ruby, and iron and titanium make blue sapphire.
Aluminum metal is made by pulling the oxygen off alumina using huge amounts of electricity.
rankWhy: The ore that aluminum metal is made from. Also sandpaper grit and sapphire.

name: Iron(III) oxide
blurb: Iron gives 3 electrons, oxygen takes 2, so 2 Fe balance 3 O. This is red rust.
facts: Mars looks red because its dust is full of rusty iron minerals.
Hematite's name comes from the Greek word for blood, because the powder is blood-red.
Red ochre, an iron oxide, was among the first paints people ever used, in cave art tens of thousands of years ago.
rankWhy: Rust, and the iron ore that steel is made from.

name: Magnetite
blurb: A mix of Fe2+ and Fe3+ ions with oxygen. Naturally magnetic.
facts: Lodestones are natural magnetite magnets. Hung on a string, they pointed north and became the first compasses.
Some bacteria grow chains of tiny magnetite crystals and use them like a compass needle.

name: Copper(II) oxide
blurb: Copper gives 2, oxygen takes 2. The black tarnish on hot copper.
facts: Copper oxides give glass and pottery glazes their blue and green colors.
The first 'high-temperature' superconductors, found in 1986, are built around copper-oxide layers.

name: Copper(I) oxide
blurb: Here copper gives just its 1 loose electron, so 2 Cu per O. Red-colored.
facts: It occurs in nature as the red mineral cuprite.
In the 1920s, layers of Cu2O made some of the first rectifiers, devices that let electricity flow only one way.

name: Titanium dioxide
blurb: Titanium gives 4 electrons, enough for 2 oxygens.
uses: White pigment in paint and sunscreen.
facts: It's one of the whitest things known, so a thin layer hides what's underneath. That's why good paint covers in one coat.
The EU banned it as a food coloring, E171, in 2022.
Some self-cleaning windows use a thin TiO2 coating that breaks down dirt in sunlight.
rankWhy: The white pigment in paint, sunscreen, paper and toothpaste.

name: Zinc oxide
blurb: Zinc gives 2 electrons, oxygen takes 2.
facts: Calamine, the pink lotion for itchy rashes, is mostly zinc oxide.
ZnO turns yellow when hot and goes back to white as it cools.

name: Lithium oxide
blurb: Each lithium gives 1 electron. Oxygen has 2 empty hands, so it needs two.
facts: It forms when lithium metal burns in air, with a crimson-red flame.
Lithium-containing glass-ceramics make cooktops that don't crack when heated fast.

name: Sodium hydroxide
blurb: Na+ and OH- stuck together like magnets.
facts: Many drain cleaners are lye. It turns hair and grease into a soapy goo that washes away.
Most of it is made by running electricity through salt water, which makes chlorine gas at the same time.
Dissolving it in water makes the water get very hot.

name: Calcium carbonate
blurb: Ca2+ stuck like a magnet to carbonate (CO3 2-), a carbon holding 3 oxygens.
uses: Limestone, chalk, shells; raw material for cement.
facts: The White Cliffs of Dover are chalk made from the shells of tiny ocean algae.
The Great Pyramid was built mostly from limestone blocks.
Antacid tablets like Tums are calcium carbonate.

name: Sodium bicarbonate
blurb: Na+ and HCO3- stuck together like magnets.
facts: When heated, baking soda gives off CO2 gas. Those bubbles make cakes rise.
Add vinegar and it fizzes right away, releasing the same CO2 much faster.

name: Lithium hydride
blurb: Here hydrogen takes an electron (H-) instead of holding hands.
facts: It's light and full of hydrogen, which makes it good at stopping neutrons. It was used as shielding for space nuclear reactors.
A version made with heavy hydrogen, lithium deuteride, is the fuel inside hydrogen bombs.

name: Lithium cobalt oxide
blurb: Layers of cobalt oxide with charged lithium (Li+) sliding in between.
uses: Cathode in many phone and laptop batteries.
facts: John Goodenough found this battery material in 1980. He won the Nobel Prize in 2019 at age 97, the oldest winner ever.
When you charge your phone, lithium moves out of this layer and into the graphite on the other side.

name: Uranium dioxide
blurb: Uranium gives 4 electrons, enough for 2 oxygens.
facts: One fuel pellet, about the size of a fingertip, holds about as much energy as a ton of coal.
The pellets are a ceramic, not a metal, so they can handle very high heat without melting.

name: Diamond
blurb: Every carbon holds 4 other carbons, one per hand, in a 3D web. No weak direction, so it's the hardest natural material.
uses: Cutting tools, grinding grit, gems, heat spreaders.
facts: Diamond moves heat better than any other natural material, about 5 times better than copper.
A diamond is just carbon. Heat it enough in air and it burns away into CO2.
Most natural diamonds formed about 100 miles underground and are over a billion years old.

name: Graphite
blurb: Each carbon holds 3 neighbors in flat hexagon sheets. Its 4th electron roams across the sheet, so graphite carries electricity. Sheets slide over each other.

lens.nexus: Char at your plant is messy, graphite-like carbon: what's left when hydrogen is stripped off and rings join.
lens.rocket: Carbon-carbon (graphite fibers set in carbon) protects the hottest front edges.

facts: Pencil 'lead' has never had lead in it. Early users thought graphite was a kind of lead.
A single sheet of graphite is graphene. It was first peeled off with sticky tape in 2004, and that work won the 2010 Nobel Prize.

name: Silicon crystal
blurb: Each silicon holds 4 others, like diamond. But the grips are weaker, so a few electrons can break free: a semiconductor.
facts: Silicon is the second most common element in Earth's crust, after oxygen.
Chip-grade silicon is about 99.9999999% pure. That's one stray atom per billion.

name: Silica (quartz)
blurb: Each silicon holds 4 oxygens. Each oxygen uses its 2 hands to bridge 2 silicons. That shared web gives the 1:2 ratio.
uses: Glass, sand, quartz crystals, optical fiber.

lens.rocket: The Shuttle's tiles were silica fibers and mostly air, so they blocked heat extremely well. Starship's tiles are reportedly a silica-based ceramic too.
lens.nexus: Silica is a building block of clay and zeolite catalysts.

facts: The quartz crystal in a watch vibrates 32,768 times per second to keep time.
Glass is silica that cooled too fast for its atoms to line up into crystals.

name: Silicon carbide
blurb: Si and C take turns, each using all 4 hands to hold the other kind. Diamond-like hardness.
uses: Grinding grit, EV power chips, brake discs, armor.
facts: Natural SiC is extremely rare. Henri Moissan found it at a meteor crater in Arizona, and the gem moissanite is named after him.
The Tesla Model 3 was one of the first mass-market cars to use SiC power chips.

name: Boron nitride
blurb: B and N take turns in hexagon sheets, like graphite. Boron's gap gets filled by nitrogen's spare pair.
facts: The flat form is called 'white graphite.' It's slippery like graphite, but white and doesn't carry electricity.
Squeezed into a diamond-like form, it's one of the hardest materials known, and it can cut steel that wears diamond down.

name: Gallium arsenide
blurb: Ga (3 outer electrons) and As (5) average 4, so they build a silicon-like crystal.

lens.rocket: Multi-junction gallium arsenide solar cells power many satellites, especially high-power ones.

facts: Gallium metal melts at about 30 °C, so it can melt in your hand.
Electrons move faster in GaAs than in silicon, so it's used in radio chips inside phones.

name: Tungsten carbide
blurb: Carbon atoms tucked into a tungsten grid; extremely hard.
uses: Drill bits, cutting tools, ballpoint pen tips.
facts: Most drill bits and saw tips labeled 'carbide' are tungsten carbide.
To make tools, the powder is pressed and baked with a little cobalt that acts like glue.

name: Zeolite (ZSM-5 type)
blurb: A silica web with some silicons swapped for aluminum. Each swap leaves a charge that holds a sodium or an acidic hydrogen inside molecule-sized holes.

lens.nexus: Zeolite powder in your plant's hot bath snaps chains at acid spots inside its holes, steering products toward gasoline/diesel-length molecules.

facts: Zeolite means 'boiling stone' in Greek. Heat the natural mineral and it hisses out steam from water trapped inside.
Its holes are about the size of a single molecule, so it can sort molecules by size like a sieve.

name: Copper metal
blurb: Metals don't hold hands one-to-one. Each copper atom tosses its 1 loose (4s) electron into a shared 'sea' drifting through the grid. A voltage pushes that sea along: current.

lens.rocket: Raptor's combustion chamber is reportedly a copper alloy (metal mix). Copper moves heat well, carrying it into the methane flowing through the cooling channels.

facts: The Statue of Liberty's skin is copper about as thick as two pennies. Its green coat is weathered copper.
Copper was one of the first metals people used, about 10,000 years ago.

name: Iron metal
blurb: Iron atoms in a grid, sharing their outer electrons as a sea. Some electrons (d-electrons) also line up into magnetic zones.
facts: Earth's core is mostly iron, mixed with nickel.
Iron in your blood carries oxygen, and it's part of why blood is red.
Iron is made in big stars. When a star's core turns to iron, it can't get more energy and collapses.

name: Aluminum metal
blurb: Each atom tosses 3 outer electrons into the sea. Light atoms, strong hold.

lens.rocket: Aluminum alloys (including aluminum-lithium) are used for Falcon 9's propellant tanks.

facts: Before 1886, aluminum was so hard to make that it cost more than gold. Napoleon III served his most honored guests with aluminum forks.
The tip of the Washington Monument is a small aluminum pyramid, set in place in 1884.
Recycling aluminum takes only about 5% of the energy needed to make new metal.

name: Nickel metal
blurb: A metal grid whose surface atoms can grab other molecules and loosen their grips.

lens.rocket: The Sabatier catalyst (helper): CO2 and H2 meet on nickel's surface and leave as methane and water.
lens.nexus: Nickel catalysts add hydrogen to oils (hydrotreating).

facts: The US 5-cent 'nickel' is actually 75% copper and only 25% nickel.
One of the world's biggest nickel mining areas, Sudbury in Canada, sits in an ancient meteorite crater.

name: Platinum metal
blurb: Surface atoms grab molecules just hard enough to break and rebuild their grips, then let go.

lens.nexus: In refinery reformers, platinum catalysts reshape naphtha into high-octane ring molecules (aromatics).

facts: Platinum is denser than gold. A platinum bar weighs about 10% more than a gold bar the same size.
From 1889 to 2019, the official kilogram was a metal cylinder made mostly of platinum.

name: Sodium metal
blurb: Each atom has 1 very loose outer electron. Soft enough to cut with a knife, and reacts violently with water.
uses: Coolant in some reactors, sodium lamps.
facts: Sodium metal is stored under oil, because it reacts with the moisture in air.
The orange glow of old street lights comes from sodium vapor.

name: Lithium metal
blurb: The lightest metal. Each atom gives 1 loose outer electron to the sea.
facts: Lithium is so light it floats on water, and even on oil.
It's one of the few elements made in the Big Bang itself.

name: Titanium metal
blurb: A strong metal grid at about 60% the density of steel. It forms a tough oxide (rust-like) skin.

lens.rocket: Titanium is used for high-strength fittings and, on Falcon 9, its grid fins.

facts: The SR-71 Blackbird was made mostly of titanium, some of it quietly bought from the Soviet Union.
Bone can grow right onto titanium and lock it in place.

name: Tungsten metal
blurb: Its atoms grip each other very hard: the highest melting point of any metal (3,422 °C).
uses: Filaments, heavy alloys, X-ray tube targets.
facts: Tungsten is almost exactly as dense as gold. Crooks have made fake gold bars with tungsten hidden inside.
Its symbol W comes from 'wolfram,' its other name.

name: Gold metal
blurb: Gold holds its outer electron tightly, so it barely reacts. Relativity effects shift its color to yellow.
uses: Electronics contacts, jewelry, spacecraft thermal films.
facts: All the gold ever mined would fit in a cube about 22 meters (74 feet) on each side.
Astronaut helmet visors have a super-thin gold layer to block harsh sunlight and heat.
Gold can be hammered so thin that light shines through it, glowing green.

name: Silver metal
blurb: Each atom gives 1 loose electron to the sea. The best electrical conductor of all elements.
facts: Black tarnish on silver is silver sulfide, made from tiny traces of sulfur gas in the air.
Silver kills many germs, so it's used in some bandages.

name: Magnesium metal
blurb: Each atom gives 2 outer electrons to the sea. Very light.
facts: At the center of every chlorophyll molecule, the green stuff in leaves, sits one magnesium atom.
Burning magnesium is very hard to put out, and water can make the fire worse.

name: Zinc metal
blurb: 2 outer electrons per atom; it corrodes in place of steel.
facts: US pennies made since 1982 are 97.5% zinc with a thin copper coat.
Your body needs a little zinc for healing and for your senses of taste and smell.

name: Carbon steel
blurb: Small carbon atoms wedge into gaps in the iron grid and pin its layers so they can't slide. A trace of carbon makes iron several times stronger.
facts: The world makes far more steel than any other metal, close to 2 billion tons a year.
Blacksmiths harden steel by heating it red-hot and plunging it into water, called quenching.

name: Stainless steel (304-type)
blurb: Chromium in the iron grid reacts with air to form a thin chromium-oxide skin. The skin heals itself and stops rust. Nickel keeps it tough at super-cold temperatures.

lens.rocket: Starship's hull began as 304L stainless. SpaceX has since moved to its own alloy, reportedly called '30X'. Steel stays strong at -183 °C (liquid oxygen) and weakens less than aluminum when hot.
lens.nexus: Stainless is common for reactors and piping where corrosion matters.

facts: Harry Brearley made one of the first stainless steels in 1913 while looking for better gun barrels.
Stainless isn't fully rust-proof. Salt water and deep scratches can still leave rust spots.

name: Bronze
blurb: Bigger tin atoms in the copper grid make the layers harder to slide. So it's harder than either metal alone.
facts: Bronze gave its name to the Bronze Age, which began more than 5,000 years ago.
Copper alloys like bronze barely spark when struck, so they're used for tools around flammable gas.

name: Brass
blurb: Zinc atoms take some copper spots in the grid. That makes it harder and easier to machine.
facts: Germs die off on brass surfaces within hours, which makes it a good choice for door handles.
It's easy to cut and shape, which is why so many keys are made of brass.

name: Aluminum-lithium alloy
blurb: Lithium is the lightest metal. Each percent of lithium cuts density by about 3% and stiffens the alloy.

lens.rocket: Falcon 9's tanks and the Shuttle's later external tank used aluminum-lithium alloy.

facts: Lithium metal is about 5 times lighter than aluminum, so a little goes a long way.
The Shuttle's later 'super lightweight' tank switched to aluminum-lithium. It was thousands of pounds lighter, so more cargo could go to the space station.

name: Inconel (nickel superalloy)
blurb: A nickel-chromium grid that stays strong and resists oxygen attack even red-hot.

lens.rocket: Nickel superalloys are used in rocket turbopumps and engine parts that see hot, oxygen-rich gas.

facts: The X-15 rocket plane's skin was Inconel X, built to survive the heat of flying more than six times the speed of sound.
It's hard to machine because it stays strong even as the cutting tool heats it up.

name: Solder (tin-silver-copper)
blurb: Mostly tin, which melts low. Small additions make the joint stronger.
facts: Classic tin-lead solder melts at 183 °C, lower than either tin or lead alone.
Old solder was mostly tin and lead. Lead-free solder took over after Europe's RoHS rules began in 2006.

name: Sucrose (table sugar)
blurb: One glucose ring and one fructose ring each give up a hand to the same oxygen. That oxygen bridge holds the two rings together like a clasp.
uses: Sweetening food and drinks, baking, candy, making ethanol from cane juice.
facts: Most of the world's sugar comes from sugarcane. Most of the rest comes from sugar beets.
About 185 million tonnes of sugar were made worldwide in 2017.
Heat it to about 170 °C and it starts to break apart into caramel.

details.what: Two smaller sugars, glucose and fructose, joined into one molecule. It's the white sugar in your kitchen.
details.where: In the sugar bowl, in sodas, candy and baked goods. Plants make it to move energy from leaves to roots and fruit.
details.bonds: Every carbon holds 4 hands and every oxygen 2. Lots of O-H groups stick out, and water grabs onto them. That's why sugar dissolves so easily.
details.extra: Your gut can't use it as-is. An enzyme (a helper protein) snips the oxygen bridge back into glucose and fructose first.

rankWhy: Table sugar, one of the biggest farm products on Earth.

name: Fructose (fruit sugar)
blurb: Same atoms as glucose, arranged differently. The carbons, oxygens and hydrogens still fill every hand, just in a different pattern.
uses: Fruit, honey, high-fructose corn syrup, sweetening drinks.
facts: It's the sweetest sugar found in nature, about 1.2 to 1.8 times as sweet as table sugar.
Honey has a little more fructose than glucose.
French chemist Augustin-Pierre Dubrunfaut discovered it in 1847.

details.what: A simple sugar with the same formula as glucose, C6H12O6. Same parts, different build.
details.where: In fruit, honey and many sodas. Half of every table sugar molecule is fructose.
details.bonds: Its ring holds one oxygen and five carbons, with O-H groups on the outside. Those O-H groups grab water, so it dissolves fast.
details.extra: Two molecules with the same atoms but a different shape are called isomers. Glucose and fructose are a classic pair.

name: Glycine
blurb: The middle carbon uses its 4 hands on a nitrogen group, a carbon-oxygen group and two hydrogens. Nitrogen fills its 3 hands, and each oxygen fills its 2.
uses: Building block of every protein; also used in food flavoring and supplements.
facts: It's the only common amino acid with no left-handed or right-handed version.
About 35% of the amino acids in collagen, the protein in skin and tendons, are glycine.
In 2016 the Rosetta spacecraft found glycine in the gas around comet 67P.

details.what: The simplest amino acid. Amino acids are the beads your body strings together to make proteins.
details.where: In every protein you eat or are made of. It's especially common in skin, tendons and gelatin.
details.bonds: One end has a nitrogen with hydrogens (the amino part). The other end has the acid group, a carbon holding two oxygens. Those two ends link up with other amino acids like train cars.
details.extra: It tastes mildly sweet. Its name comes from the Greek word for sweet.

rankWhy: The simplest building block of the proteins you're made of.

name: Alanine
blurb: It's glycine with one hydrogen swapped for a CH3 group. The middle carbon still holds 4 hands: nitrogen, the acid group, a hydrogen and that CH3.
uses: Building block of proteins; a fuel your muscles and liver trade back and forth.
facts: Adolph Strecker first made it in 1850 from acetaldehyde, ammonia and hydrogen cyanide.
Because its middle carbon holds four different things, it comes in left- and right-handed versions. Life builds proteins with the left-handed one.

details.what: One of the 20 amino acids your body uses to build proteins.
details.where: In nearly every protein in meat, eggs, beans and your own muscles.
details.bonds: Same two ends as glycine: a nitrogen group and an acid group. Those ends let it link into long protein chains.
details.extra: Its name was made from 'aldehyde,' the chemical it was first made from.

name: Caffeine
blurb: Two rings of carbon and nitrogen share an edge. Nitrogen fills its 3 hands inside the rings, and some carbons use a double hand to an oxygen.
uses: Coffee, tea, energy drinks, some pain relievers.
facts: It's the world's most widely used mind-affecting drug.
Plants make it as a natural bug killer. It can paralyze and kill insects that chew on them.
An 8 oz cup of coffee has about 80 to 100 mg. The FDA says up to 400 mg a day appears safe for most healthy adults.

details.what: A small, bitter molecule made by coffee, tea and cacao plants. It keeps you alert.
details.where: In coffee, tea, cola, energy drinks and chocolate.
details.bonds: The two rings are flat and stiff because electrons spread across them. Small CH3 groups hang off three of the nitrogens.
details.extra: It works by blocking the 'you're tired' signal in your brain, a molecule called adenosine.

rankWhy: The world's most widely used mind-affecting drug, in coffee and tea.

name: Aspirin
blurb: A benzene ring, a six-carbon ring with alternating double hands, carries two groups. One is an acid group, the other an acetyl group hooked on through an oxygen.
uses: Pain and fever relief; low doses used for some heart patients.
facts: Felix Hoffmann at Bayer made the first pure sample on 10 August 1897.
Bayer started selling it under the name Aspirin in 1899.
Willow bark contains a natural cousin of it, salicin. People chewed willow bark for pain long before aspirin.

details.what: A pain reliever made by adding an acetyl group to salicylic acid, a chemical related to one in willow bark.
details.where: In medicine cabinets, as tablets for headaches, fever and inflammation.
details.bonds: The ring is flat and stable. The acetyl group is held by an oxygen bridge that water can slowly snap. That's why old aspirin can smell like vinegar.
details.extra: It blocks an enzyme the body uses to make pain and swelling signals.

rankWhy: The classic pain reliever, sold for over 120 years.

name: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid)
blurb: A five-member ring with one oxygen in it. Two ring carbons share a double hand, and a third holds an oxygen with a double hand. The O-H groups on the double-handed carbons give up hydrogen easily. That makes it an acid.
uses: Vitamin supplements, keeping food from browning, preventing scurvy.
facts: Humans, other apes and monkeys, guinea pigs and most bats can't make their own. Most other animals can.
In 1747 ship's surgeon James Lind gave sailors with scurvy oranges and lemons. It was one of the first controlled experiments.
Albert Szent-Györgyi won the 1937 Nobel Prize, partly for his work on vitamin C.

details.what: A vitamin your body needs to build collagen, the protein that holds skin and blood vessels together.
details.where: In citrus fruit, peppers, strawberries and broccoli. Also added to juices and foods.
details.bonds: It gives away electrons easily. That lets it protect other molecules from oxygen, which is why it's added to food.
details.extra: Its name means 'no scurvy.' Scurvy is the disease you get without it.

rankWhy: Vitamin C. You can't make it, so you have to eat it.

name: Citric acid
blurb: A short chain of carbons carrying three acid groups. In each acid group a carbon holds one oxygen with a double hand and another with a single hand.
uses: Sour flavor in drinks and candy, cleaning products, preserving food.
facts: Most of it is made by a mold, Aspergillus niger, fed on sugar.
The world made over 2 million tons of it in 2018, more than half in China.
Every cell in your body runs a chain of reactions named after it, the citric acid cycle.

details.what: The acid that makes lemons and limes sour.
details.where: In citrus fruit, sodas, sour candy, bath bombs and descaling cleaners.
details.bonds: Its three acid groups can each let go of a hydrogen. That makes it a good grabber of metal atoms, so it dissolves scale and hard-water stains.
details.extra: Lemons and limes can be up to 8% citric acid by dry weight.

rankWhy: Lemon sourness. Added to drinks, candy and cleaners.

name: Isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol)
blurb: Three carbons in a bent row. The middle carbon uses one hand on an oxygen, and that oxygen's other hand holds a hydrogen.
uses: Rubbing alcohol, hand sanitizer, cleaning electronics, solvent in labs and factories.
facts: It's made by adding water to propylene.
Rubbing alcohol is usually 60 to 70% in water. The water helps it get into germs.

details.what: A simple alcohol, a cousin of ethanol with one more carbon.
details.where: In first-aid kits, wipes, hand sanitizer and screen cleaners.
details.bonds: The O-H group grabs water, and the carbon part grabs oils. So it mixes with both and cleans greasy dirt off fast.
details.extra: It evaporates quickly and leaves almost nothing behind, which is why it's used on circuit boards.

name: Lactic acid
blurb: Three carbons in a row. The middle one holds an O-H, and the end carbon is an acid group holding two oxygens.
uses: Yogurt and sourdough tang, food preservative, making PLA plastic.
facts: It gives yogurt, kefir and sourdough bread their sour taste.
PLA, a plastic used in 3D printing, is made from lactic acid instead of oil.

details.what: A small acid made by bacteria when they ferment sugar. Your muscles make it too when working hard.
details.where: In yogurt, sauerkraut, sour beer and pickles.
details.bonds: The acid group lets go of a hydrogen, which makes food sour and slows the growth of germs that spoil it.
details.extra: Its middle carbon holds four different things, so it comes in left- and right-handed versions.

name: Acetaminophen (paracetamol)
blurb: A benzene ring with an O-H on one side and an N-H group on the opposite side. The nitrogen uses its third hand on an acetyl group.
facts: It's called acetaminophen in the US, Canada and Japan, and paracetamol in most other places.
Too much of it is the leading cause of sudden liver failure in many countries.

details.what: A common pain and fever reliever.
details.where: In medicine cabinets and in many cold and flu mixes.
details.bonds: The flat ring holds the two groups in place. The liver breaks it down, and a big overdose makes a harmful leftover the liver can't clear.
details.extra: It isn't a strong anti-swelling drug like aspirin or ibuprofen.

rankWhy: One of the most-used pain and fever medicines.

name: Ibuprofen
blurb: A benzene ring with a branched carbon chain on one side and an acid group on the other. Every carbon fills its 4 hands.
facts: Stewart Adams and John Nicholson found it at Boots in Nottingham, England, in 1961.
Adams tested an early dose on his own hangover.

details.what: A pain reliever that also calms swelling.
details.where: In medicine cabinets as Advil, Motrin or store brands.
details.bonds: The ring and the branched chain are oily and shun water. The acid group on the other end is the part that mixes with water.
details.extra: Like aspirin, it blocks the enzyme that makes swelling and pain signals.

name: Glycerol (glycerin)
blurb: Three carbons in a row, each with an O-H group. Every hand is held.
uses: Soaps, lotions, food sweetener, making nitroglycerin.
facts: Every fat or oil molecule is three fatty acids hung on a glycerol backbone.
Making soap or biodiesel from fats sets glycerol free as a leftover.
Adding nitric acid to it makes nitroglycerin, used in explosives and heart medicine.

details.where: In soaps, lotions, toothpaste, and as a sweetener and moisture keeper in foods.
details.bonds: Three O-H groups grab water strongly. That's why it keeps skin and foods moist.
details.extra: Swedish chemist Carl Wilhelm Scheele first found it. He called it the sweet part of fat.

name: Phosphoric acid
blurb: A phosphorus in the middle holds four oxygens, one with a double hand. Three of those oxygens hold a hydrogen with their other hand. Here phosphorus uses 5 hands, more than its usual 3.
uses: Fertilizer, cola tang, rust removal, food additive.
facts: About 90% of it goes into fertilizer.
It gives colas their sharp, sour bite.

details.what: An acid built around one phosphorus atom.
details.where: In fertilizer, colas, and rust removers.
details.bonds: The three hydrogens can each let go, one at a time. Phosphorus is big enough to hold more than 3 hands' worth of bonds.
details.extra: Plants need phosphorus to make DNA and to move energy around. Fertilizer is how farms supply it.

rankWhy: Mostly goes into fertilizer. Farms need phosphorus to grow food.

name: Vinyl chloride
blurb: Two carbons hold a double hand. One carbon uses its last hand on a chlorine. Open that double hand and the molecules link into PVC.
uses: Making PVC pipe, siding and flooring.
facts: Nearly all of it is used to make PVC.
In 2023 a train derailed in Ohio, spilling about 100,000 gallons of hazardous chemicals including vinyl chloride.

details.what: A small gas that is the building block of PVC plastic.
details.where: You meet it as PVC: pipes, window frames, flooring, cable coating.
details.bonds: The double hand between the carbons can open up. Each carbon then grabs a neighbor molecule, building a long chain.
details.extra: It's flammable and causes cancer, so it's handled in closed systems.
